questions.q: In a mortgage, who is the mortgagor?
choices: The lender who advances the money
The borrower who grants the mortgage
The insurer that guarantees the loan
The broker who arranges the loan
questions.explain: The mortgagor is the borrower: they grant the mortgage as security and receive the loan. The mortgagee is the lender.

questions.q: An investor borrows at 5% to buy a property earning 8%. What is this an example of?
questions.explain: Borrowing at a lower rate than the investment earns magnifies the return on equity: positive leverage.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Why real estate runs on debt

questions.q: What does a lender-investor primarily want from a mortgage loan?
choices: Use of the property and long-term appreciation
A predictable return plus return of capital
A share of the rental income the property earns
Ownership of the property when the loan matures
questions.explain: Lenders want regular, predictable interest and the scheduled return of principal, protected by security.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Why real estate runs on debt

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three parts of a mortgage rate from the lender's point of view?
choices: A base return on the capital
A charge for managing the loan
questions.explain: The three parts are a base return, a risk premium and a payment toward management costs.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · The capital market and interest rates

questions.q: Why do mortgages usually pay more than government bonds of a similar term?
choices: Mortgages are guaranteed by the federal government
They're riskier, less liquid, more work
Bonds always have much longer terms
Bonds need more active management by investors
questions.explain: Mortgages carry more default risk, are harder to sell and require more administration, so investors demand a higher yield.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · The capital market and interest rates

questions.q: How do institutional lenders usually handle extra risk on an individual loan?
choices: Charge that borrower a higher rate
Ask CMHC to set the rate
questions.explain: They tend to keep the market rate and adjust non-rate terms such as term, amortization or loan-to-value.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · The capital market and interest rates

questions.q: What happens in the secondary mortgage market?
choices: Existing mortgages are bought and sold
The Bank of Canada sets mortgage rates
questions.explain: The secondary market trades existing mortgages: buyers acquire the right to the borrower's payments.

questions.q: What is the reinvestment problem for small mortgage investors?
choices: Small payments can't fund new loans
They can't sell their mortgages at all
Rates always fall after the loan is made
questions.explain: A small lender's monthly payments are too small to make a new mortgage, so they sit in lower-yielding accounts.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Why mortgages were hard for small investors

questions.q: Who created NHA Mortgage-Backed Securities, and when?
questions.explain: CMHC created NHA MBS in 1986: pools of insured residential mortgages sold in small units, paid monthly.

questions.q: How often do Canada Mortgage Bond holders receive interest?
questions.explain: CMBs, issued by the Canada Housing Trust since 2001, pay fixed interest every six months.

questions.q: What share of its net income can a qualifying MIC pass through to investors?
questions.explain: Under the Income Tax Act rules, a MIC can pass on 100% of its net income to its shareholders.

questions.q: After the 1930s Depression, which repayment plan became standard?
choices: Variable rate mortgages tied to prime
questions.explain: Interest-only loans left principal at risk, so lenders moved to long-term, fully amortized constant payment loans.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · A short history of Canadian mortgages

questions.q: Why did partially amortized (short-term) mortgages emerge in the 1970s?
choices: To comply with the Interest Act
questions.explain: Rising rates exposed lenders to interest rate risk. Short terms let rates reset, sharing the risk with borrowers.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · A short history of Canadian mortgages

questions.q: Since June 2021, what is the minimum qualifying rate under the stress test?
questions.explain: The greater of 5.25% or the contract rate plus 2%, subject to periodic review.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Federal rule changes you should recognize

questions.q: Since December 2024, what is the price cap for an insured mortgage?
questions.explain: The cap rose from $1 million to $1.5 million. Homes at $1.5 million or more need 20% down and can't be insured.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Federal rule changes you should recognize

questions.q: Since 2016, what minimum down payment applies to the part of an insured purchase price above $500,000?
questions.explain: 5% on the first $500,000 and 10% on the portion above that (up to $1.5 million).
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Federal rule changes you should recognize

questions.q: What's the maximum loan-to-value for a conventional mortgage at a federally regulated lender?
questions.explain: 80%. Above that, the loan is high-ratio and must be insured (up to 95%).

questions.q: Who pays for mortgage default insurance, and who does it protect?
choices: Lender pays; it protects the borrower
Borrower pays; it protects the lender
Government pays; it protects the lender
questions.explain: The borrower pays the premium (usually added to the loan), but the insurance protects the lender against default losses.

questions.q: What makes a mortgage the "first" mortgage?
choices: It's the largest loan on title
It has the lowest interest rate
questions.explain: Rank depends on registration order, not size. Later mortgages are junior mortgages.

questions.q: Which type of institution has been the largest source of mortgage funds in Canada since 1979?
questions.explain: Chartered banks, mainly through residential lending. Trust companies led from 1967 to 1978.

questions.q: What is a monoline lender?
choices: A lender serving only commercial clients
A credit union with a single branch
A lender offering one fixed rate
questions.explain: Monolines (e.g. MCAP, First National) focus only on mortgages, have no branches and deal only through brokers.

questions.q: Where did life insurance companies shift their mortgage lending?
questions.explain: Fixed residential yields didn't protect policyholders from inflation, so insurers moved to non-residential loans and equity participation.

questions.q: Trust companies were classic "spread lenders". What does that mean?
choices: They lent only on spread-out rural farmland
They matched deposit and loan terms for a margin
They spread each loan among many co-lenders
They charged one identical rate across Canada
questions.explain: They matched, say, 5-year GICs with 5-year mortgages to lock in a spread of about 1.5%.

questions.q: How do payments behave on a straight line principal reduction loan?
questions.explain: Equal principal each period plus interest on a shrinking balance, so total payments fall. The largest are at the start.

questions.q: Which describes an interest accruing loan?
choices: Interest paid monthly, principal at the end
No payments until the loan matures
questions.explain: Nothing is paid during the term; interest is added to the balance and everything is due at maturity.

questions.q: Where are interest-only loans most commonly used?
questions.explain: Developers keep financing costs low during construction and repay from sales on completion.

questions.q: On a constant payment mortgage, what are the early payments made up of?
questions.explain: The balance is largest at the start, so early payments are mostly interest. The principal portion grows over time.

questions.q: What makes a mortgage partially amortized?
choices: The term is longer than the amortization
The amortization is longer than the term
It has no amortization period at all
questions.explain: Payments are based on a long amortization, but the contract ends sooner, leaving a balance to repay or refinance.

questions.q: What is a balloon payment?
choices: The term is longer than the amortization period
The amortization is longer than the term
The term and the amortization are equal
It has no amortization period whatsoever
questions.explain: Any principal paid over and above the regular payments, including the balance due at the end of the term.

questions.q: Since December 2024, what's the maximum amortization for an insured mortgage to a first-time buyer?
questions.explain: 30 years for all first-time buyers and buyers of new builds; 25 years for other insured mortgages.

questions.q: How is an accelerated biweekly payment calculated?
choices: Half the monthly payment, every two weeks
The full monthly payment, every two weeks
A quarter of the monthly payment, weekly
questions.explain: Half the monthly payment paid 26 times a year: the equivalent of 13 monthly payments.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Making a mortgage disappear faster

questions.q: Accelerated biweekly payments add the equivalent of how much each year?
questions.explain: 26 half-payments = 13 monthly payments, so one extra monthly payment goes to principal each year.

questions.q: Which describes an open mortgage?
choices: A lower rate and a long term
Prepay anytime, at a higher rate
questions.explain: Open mortgages allow prepayment at any time (small fee) but carry higher rates and short terms.

questions.q: What is a convertible mortgage?
choices: A variable that auto-switches to fixed
A short closed term you can lengthen
A loan that converts into equity
A mortgage that converts to a lease
questions.explain: A short-term (often 6-month or 1-year) closed mortgage that can be converted to a longer term at current rates.

questions.q: Why are variable rate mortgages usually cheaper than fixed?
choices: The lender carries the rate risk
The borrower carries the rate risk
questions.explain: Rate changes pass to the borrower, so the lender takes less risk and charges less.

questions.q: What do fixed mortgage rates generally move with?
choices: The Bank of Canada's overnight rate
questions.explain: Fixed rates track bond yields and deposit rates of similar maturity; variable rates track prime.

questions.q: What happens under a reverse annuity mortgage?
choices: The lender pays the borrower over time
questions.explain: The lender advances payments to the (usually retired) borrower; the balance is repaid on sale, death or refinancing.

questions.q: What does a borrower get in exchange for giving a lender a share of the property's appreciation?
questions.explain: A shared appreciation mortgage trades a lower rate for a share of the gain in value.

questions.q: A home equity loan is typically limited to what percentage of value, less existing mortgages?
questions.explain: Typically up to 65% of the lower of price or appraised value, minus existing mortgage balances.

questions.q: How is construction financing usually advanced and repaid during the build?
choices: By the vendor to the purchaser
questions.explain: Funds are advanced in instalments as stages are completed, typically on an interest-only basis.

questions.q: For a blended-payment mortgage, how must the rate be stated under s.6 of the Interest Act?
choices: Yearly or half-yearly, not in advance
At any frequency the lender likes
questions.explain: Calculated yearly or half-yearly, not in advance. That's why Canadian rates are quoted with semi-annual compounding.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · The Interest Act: how rates must be quoted

questions.q: What does "not in advance" mean in an interest rate quote?
choices: Interest is charged at the period's start
Interest is charged at the period's end
Interest is waived for the first period
Interest is paid before funds advance
questions.explain: Interest accrues over the period and is charged at its end. Assume this unless told otherwise.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · The Interest Act: how rates must be quoted

questions.q: Under s.10 of the Interest Act, who can prepay, and on what terms?
choices: Any borrower at any time, without a penalty
An individual after 5 years + 3 months' interest
A corporation after 3 years, with no fee at all
An individual after 1 year, with no penalty
questions.explain: An individual whose mortgage runs more than 5 years can pay it off after 5 years with three months' interest.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · The Interest Act: how rates must be quoted

questions.q: What is the periodic rate for j₄ = 10%?
questions.explain: i = jₘ ÷ m = 10% ÷ 4 = 2.5% per quarter.

questions.q: A loan charges 0.5% per period at a nominal rate of 6%. How many compounding periods are there per year?
Which rate is the effective annual rate?
questions.explain: j₁, the nominal rate compounded once a year, is the effective annual rate.

questions.q: Which mode should the HP 10bII+ be in for this course?
questions.explain: End mode: payments at the end of each period. If BEG shows on the display, switch it off.

questions.q: Which calculators are allowed in the exam room?
choices: Only the HP 10bII+ model, nothing else
Any calculator app on a smartphone
questions.explain: Silent, cordless, hand-held calculators that are not both alphanumeric and programmable.

questions.q: From the borrower's perspective, how are the keys signed in a mortgage problem?
choices: PV negative, PMT and FV positive
PV positive, PMT and FV negative
questions.explain: Money received (the loan) is positive; payments and balances paid out are negative. Reverse it for the lender.

questions.q: A loan has monthly payments and a rate of j₂ = 6%. What must you do before solving?
choices: Enter 6 in I/YR with P/YR set to 2
Convert the rate to an equivalent j₁₂
questions.explain: N, I/YR and PMT must share a frequency. Monthly payments → convert j₂ to j₁₂.

questions.q: There are no payments in a problem. What sets the frequency for N and I/YR?
choices: The size of the loan amount
questions.explain: With no payment frequency, the compounding frequency of the given rate drives the problem.

questions.q: Land bought for $250,000 rises 0.75% a month for 4 years. What is it worth then?
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Future and present value of a lump sum

questions.q: What should you pay today for $1,000,000 due in 5 years, to earn j₁₂ = 8%?
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Future and present value of a lump sum

questions.q: Which condition must hold to treat a problem as a simple lump sum?
questions.explain: There must be no payments between PV and FV (PMT = 0).
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · Future and present value of a lump sum

questions.q: What is a sinking fund?
choices: Regular deposits for a future purpose
A reserve to cover loan defaults
A lender account for property taxes
questions.explain: A series of regular deposits accumulating money for a specific future need, like replacing equipment.

questions.q: What is the monthly interest-only payment on $2,000,000 at j₁₂ = 7%?
When are two interest rates equivalent?
choices: When they have the same nominal rate
When they have the same effective rate
questions.explain: Equivalent rates give the same amount owing for the same loan and time: the same j₁.

questions.q: What j₁₂ is equivalent to j₂ = 5%?
A lender charges j₁₂ = 6%. What j₂ must it disclose under the Interest Act?
Lender A offers j₂ = 6%; Lender B offers j₁₂ = 5.94%. Which costs less?
choices: Lender A, with the lower j₁
They can't be compared at all
questions.explain: A's effective rate is 6.09%; B's is about 6.10%. Compare effective rates, not headline numbers.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you re-key a rate you just converted on the calculator?
choices: You lose precision and risk typos
It reverses the sign of PV
questions.explain: Use the converted rate straight from memory to keep full accuracy.

questions.q: What effective annual rate is equivalent to 0.5% per month?
How did the court resolve Haptom v. Pahl (24% "per annum" with $3,000/month interest-only)?
choices: The lender kept every one of the $3,000 payments
It sided with the borrowers; overpayment credited
It voided the whole loan as a criminal interest rate
It reset the rate to 24% per annum, compounded monthly
questions.explain: Monthly payments of $3,000 exceeded 24% compounded annually; the court recalculated and credited the borrowers.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · A licensee case: get the rate wording right

questions.q: What's the monthly payment on $500,000 at j₂ = 5% over 25 years?
questions.explain: Convert to j₁₂ 4.948699%, N 300, PV 500,000, FV 0 → PMT $2,908.02. ($2,922.95 is the mistake of treating 5% as j₁₂.)

questions.q: A buyer can pay $3,000/month at j₂ = 6% over 25 years. What's the maximum loan?
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · 2. Loan amount (what a payment will support)

questions.q: If rates rise and a borrower's payment stays the same, what happens to the loan they can support?
questions.explain: More of each payment goes to interest, so the same payment supports a smaller loan.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · 2. Loan amount (what a payment will support)

questions.q: Solving for N, the calculator shows "no Solution". What does that mean?
choices: The interest rate entered is too low
The payment never repays the loan
The loan is already fully amortized
questions.explain: The payment isn't large enough to ever pay off the loan at that rate.

questions.q: After calculating the payment, what must you do before finding the outstanding balance?
questions.explain: Re-enter the payment exactly as rounded in the contract (negative), then use INPUT and AMORT.

questions.q: After N INPUT ■ AMORT, what does the third press of "=" show?
choices: The principal paid in the range
The balance after the last payment
The interest paid in the range
questions.explain: Principal, then interest, then the outstanding balance after the last payment in the range.

questions.q: Which keystrokes give the interest paid in the second year of a monthly mortgage?
questions.explain: Year 2 is payments 13 to 24.
questions.ref: Lesson 12 · 6. Principal and interest over a range

questions.q: If regular payments are rounded up, how does the final payment of a fully amortized loan compare?
choices: It's larger than the regular payment
It's smaller than the regular payment
questions.explain: The borrower overpays slightly each time, so less is left for the final payment.

questions.q: What does lengthening the amortization period do?
choices: Has no effect on total interest
questions.explain: Smaller payments, but repayment is slower and more interest is paid overall (with diminishing benefit).
